questions.q: What defines a stabilizer code's valid logical states?
options: They are exactly the simultaneous +1 eigenstates of all of the code's stabilizer generators
They are any state that uses an odd number of physical qubits
They are defined by having zero overlap with the |0> state
They are whichever states a human chooses to label as 'logical'
questions.explain: A stabilizer code is defined precisely as the simultaneous +1 eigenspace of its stabilizer generators -- this is the general definition the bit-flip and phase-flip codes both satisfy.

questions.q: For an n-qubit code encoding k logical qubits, how many independent stabilizer generators are needed?
options: n - k
n times k
n + k
Exactly 2, regardless of n or k
questions.explain: The general rule is n-k independent generators -- matching the bit-flip code's 3 physical qubits, 1 logical qubit, and 2 stabilizer generators (3-1=2).

questions.q: What determines whether a Pauli error E is detected by a stabilizer generator S?
options: Whether E and S anticommute (ES = -SE) -- if so, measuring S flips to -1 and the error is detected
Whether E and S have the same number of qubits
Whether E was applied before or after the stabilizer was measured
Detection is random and unrelated to any algebraic property of E and S
questions.explain: Anticommutation with a stabilizer is exactly the condition that flips its measured eigenvalue from +1 to -1, which is how a syndrome is generated.

questions.q: Why is the bit-flip code's stabilizer set (built from Z operators) blind to Z errors?
options: Z errors are not Pauli operators, so the formalism doesn't apply to them
The bit-flip code actually does detect Z errors using this same stabilizer set
Z commutes with Z, so a Z error never anticommutes with a Z-type stabilizer, and no syndrome is triggered
Commutation rules only apply to X errors, never to Z errors
questions.explain: Since Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 are built from Z operators, and Z commutes with Z, a Z error never anticommutes with them -- exactly reproducing the blind spot identified by direct simulation in lesson 10.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'logical operator' from an error, even though both are Pauli operators acting on the physical qubits?
options: A logical operator commutes with every stabilizer (triggers no syndrome) while still changing the encoded logical information; an error is something you want to detect and undo
Logical operators only ever act on ancilla qubits, never on data qubits
Logical operators and errors are identical with no meaningful distinction
Errors always commute with every stabilizer, while logical operators never do
questions.explain: X_L = X1X2X3 commutes with both Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 (no syndrome triggered) while still flipping the logical qubit's value -- that combination is exactly what defines a logical operator as distinct from a detectable error.
